snippet.title: The Tinderbox: Understanding The Israeli-Palestinian Conflict
snippet.description:
THE TINDERBOX: understanding Israel/Palestine
We will never find peace unless we address the basic problem.

A rare and thought-provoking examination of both sides of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, from its catalyst to why it still rages, to what needs to happen for it to stop.

The Tinderbox combines ancient and more recent history, geopolitical problems (racism, inequality, immigration and fake truths), and psychology, with the deeply personal journey of one person forced to challenge everything they’d been taught about the conflict in Israel and Palestine.

The film also shows the human face of this conflict by hearing from a wide variety of contemporary voices, ranging from a Settler to a political member of Hamas. Today, while this conflict still rages, an American Middle East Peace Plan is in the works, and anti-Semitism and Islamophobia remain as globally controversial as ever, this film will provide context, show how history continues to play out in the daily lives of people on either side of the divide, and will empower audiences to make up their own minds.

snippet.title: The First Bow | How Humans Learned to Store Time as Power?
snippet.description:
What if the first true machine was not metal, gears, or engines - but a bent piece of wood?
 In The First Bow and How Humans Learned to Store Time as Power, we explore one of the quietest but most important thresholds in human history: the moment when force no longer had to be immediate - when energy could be stored, delayed, and released by choice.
This episode is part of ⭐ THE ARCHAEOLOGY OF TOOLS - The Tool Evolution Series - Prehistoric Innovation-  https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL_sDfDXuTiP0OgbZ9-dtOJX9Hb7xmWK8c
 A Sleepless Homo Mini-Universe, a calm, cinematic, scientific deep-time anthology tracing how our species became itself - not through destiny or drama, but through objects we shaped, lost, rediscovered, and perfected.
The bow was not just a weapon.

It was the first technology that:
• Stored energy instead of releasing it instantly
• Turned waiting into strategy
• Separated intention from action
• Required planning long before reward
• Extended the human mind forward in time
Through archaeology, experimental science, paleoenvironments, and cognitive research, this documentary follows the bow from silence and landscape, through skill, learning, inequality, and finally into something larger - a way of thinking that would later shape machines, economies, and futures.

🕯️ The story of humanity… told softly.

snippet.title: America the Fearful (Benjamin Radford)
snippet.description:
National panics about crime, immigrants, police, and societal degradation have been pervasive in the United States of the 21st century. Many of these fears begin as mere phantom fears, but are systematically amplified by social media, news media, bad actors and even well-intentioned activists. There are numerous challenges facing the U.S., but Americans must sort through which fears are legitimate threats and which are amplified exaggerations. In his latest book, America the Fearful, Benjamin Radford examines the role of fear in national panics and addresses why many Americans believe the country is in horrible shape and will continue to deteriorate (despite contradictory evidence). Political polarization, racism, sexism, economic inequality, and other social issues are examined. Combining media literacy, folklore, investigative journalism, psychology, neuroscience, and critical thinking approaches, this book reveals the powerful role that fear plays in clouding perceptions about the U.S. It not only records the repercussions of this toxic phenomenon, but also offers evidence-based solutions.

Benjamin Radford is longtime deputy editor of "Skeptical Inquirer" science magazine, and a Research Fellow with the Committee for Skeptical Inquiry, a non-profit educational organization. Over the past twenty years he has investigated dozens of mysterious and unexplained phenomena. He is author of a dozen books and thousands of articles on media and science literacy and co-host of the "Squaring the Strange" podcast.

Mr. Radford will be joining us remotely via Zoom.

snippet.title: The Entire History of Denmark Full Detailed 2 hours long Documentary
snippet.description:
Explore the entire history of Denmark in this detailed, educational documentary that traces the nation’s journey from its earliest settlers to the modern welfare state. This video provides a clear and chronological understanding of how Denmark evolved through major eras such as the Viking Age, medieval kingdoms, the Kalmar Union, the Reformation, absolutism, and the long rivalry with Sweden.

We follow Denmark’s transformation after major losses like the separation of Norway and the defeat in the Schleswig War, and we examine how the country rebuilt itself through democratic reforms, agricultural innovation, and a strong cultural awakening. Learn how Denmark navigated the world wars, developed its modern welfare model, expanded education, and became a global leader in sustainability, diplomacy, and quality of life.

This documentary brings together historical events, key figures, political changes, and cultural milestones to give you a complete and engaging understanding of Denmark’s past and present.

Perfect for history students, documentary fans, and anyone interested in Scandinavia, Vikings, European politics, or modern social systems.
Watch now and discover how Denmark became one of the world’s most admired nations.

snippet.title: Crash Course Scientific Thinking Preview
snippet.description:
Science is one of the best ways we have of understanding what’s going on around us. In Crash Course Scientific Thinking we’ll explore the foundational principles that underlie scientific thought. 

Course Description
In 7 episodes, Crash Course Scientific Thinking will teach learners the foundational principles underlying scientific thought, pulling back the curtain on processes like peer review, interrogating what makes sources reliable (or not), unpacking how consensus is reached, and revealing how scientific understanding changes over time. Ultimately, learners will gain the ability to think more critically about the scientific information they encounter in their everyday lives. 

Series Objectives
- Describe the dynamic, communal nature of science, articulating the roles of uncertainty and consensus.
- Explain the role of peer review and replication in science.
- Unpack the potential for bias and error in science and understand its self-correction mechanisms.
- Understand the role of specialization in scientific expertise.
- Interpret primary, secondary, and tertiary sources, and use lateral reading to verify claims.
- Understand basic statistical language used to describe scientific findings.

snippet.title: 19. The Mongols - Terror of the Steppe
snippet.description:
In the far east of the Eurasian steppe, the sound of hoofbeats is growing...

In this episode we travel along the vast grassland corridor of the steppe, to hear one of the most remarkable and unlikely stories from medieval history – the story of the Mongol Empire. Find out how this group of nomadic horse riders united the peoples of the Mongolian steppe, and forged them into a truly unique kind of state. Discover how they conquered much of the lands of Eurasia, and brought the distant cultures of China, Persia, the Middle East and Europe into contact. And hear the story of how the world’s largest land empire finally came apart, and left the world as we know it in its wake.

snippet.title: Europe's First Chapter: The Geological Birth Of A Continent
snippet.description:
Europe was not born in a single moment. In Expedition Europe: Birth Of A Continent, geologist Colin Devey follows the deep-time story written into Europe's rocks, seas and mountains. On the Isle of Lewis, 2.9 billion year old gneiss reveals the ancient nucleus of the continent, while Scotland's seas connect today's wildlife to the explosion of life 540 million years ago. At Loch Ness, the Great Glen Fault marks the collision of Laurentia and Baltica around 450 million years ago.

The journey continues through the Central Uplands, where the Variscides helped unite Europe around 350 million years ago and later gave rise to the coal that powered industrialization. In Portugal, 152 million year old dinosaur fossils reveal a time when Europe and North America still shared close links before the Atlantic opened around 220 million years ago. From the volcanic Azores to the Urals and the Manpupuner pillars, this documentary uncovers how Europe became a continent.

Across the Middle East, the India, and Southeast Asia, some of the world’s greatest cultures emerged through the fusion of religion, architecture, and human imagination. snippet.title: Centuries of the Bristlecone by Jonathon Keats
snippet.description:
A decade in the making, 𝘊𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘉𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘭𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘦 is a monumental artwork by artist and conceptual philosopher Jonathan Keats, commissioned by the Nevada Museum of Art in partnership with The Long Now Foundation. It is composed of two parts: a giant arboreal clock built by clockmakers Phil Abernethy and Brittany Nicole Cox, and a land art installation at Long Now's Nevada Bristlecone Preserve, home to the world's longest-living trees.

This video is also a sneak peek at 𝘌𝘭𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘛𝘪𝘮𝘦, a documentary short about the creation of 𝘊𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘴 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘉𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘭𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘦, which is in festival selection throughout 02026. Follow Long Now for future screening dates and details.

snippet.title: Everyday Extraordinary: Inspiring Critical Thinking Using Paranormal Claims (Barry Markovsky)
snippet.description:
The presentation will include readings from a book in progress, followed by an open discussion.

With this book I hope to reach a wider audience that normally wouldn’t pick up a skeptical approach. Each chapter opens with a first-person “Front Stage” account of a true extraordinary experience. Then it goes “Back Stage” to show how perfectly normal events can deceive us into inferring something supernatural. Chapter topics are familiar to most NCAS members—ghosts, astrology, dowsing, ESP, UFOs, etc. What I hope differentiates this book from other skeptical work is its approach: Telling the stories with heart and humor, and explaining what really happened instead of leaping to paranormal conclusions.

For the discussion, in addition to any feedback you’d like to offer, I’d like to brainstorm with you about strategies for maximizing the impact of this kind of endeavor. Given it’s aimed at non-scientists, what’s the optimal vocabulary level and pedagogical style? How “sciency” should it get without the risk of losing too many readers? Is there even a market for it? These are questions I struggle with every day as I write, so your input will be much appreciated.

Barry Markovsky's research areas include group processes, social psychology, social networks, methods of theory construction, experimental research, and computer simulations. His most recent work has addressed social status, identity, fairness perceptions, cooperation, and influence in small group contexts, and has developed online tools for building, evaluating, and disseminating sociological theories. He has taught courses in group processes, pseudoscience and paranormal beliefs, and theory construction. Prior to his position at the University of South Carolina, he was Sociology Program Director at the National Science Foundation and Assistant, Associate and Full Professor at the University of Iowa.

Views expressed in this video are those of the speakers and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Capital Area Skeptics.

snippet.title: The British Victory That Lost the Revolution | The Battle of Brandywine
snippet.description:
On September 11, 1777, General Howe fought the largest battle of the entire American Revolutionary War and won it completely. More soldiers engaged at the Battle of Brandywine than at Yorktown, more than at Saratoga, more than at any other engagement of the Revolution. Washington had three separate warnings that the British were flanking him. He dismissed every one. The battle lasted eleven hours. Britain won every exchange of it. Two weeks later, Philadelphia fell. And within six weeks, the war turned permanently against Britain in a way that nothing Howe had achieved at Brandywine could prevent or reverse.
This documentary tells the full story of the Battle of Brandywine from the ground up: the strategic stakes of the 1777 campaign, Howe's intelligence operation and the night march that bypassed Washington's entire defensive line, the eleven hours of fighting at Birmingham Meeting House and Chadds Ford, the men who kept the Continental Army alive in the retreat, the fall of Philadelphia, the disaster at Saratoga, and the French alliance that followed. It traces the complete chain of consequence from Brandywine to Yorktown and asks the question no existing treatment has answered directly: what does a general do with a victory that changes nothing?

CHAPTERS
00:00 Introduction
01:14 The Prize and the Plan
15:03 What General Howe Knew
27:58 Eleven Hours
46:56 The Men Who Kept the Revolution Alive
1:04:34 The Hollow City
1:23:15 The Long Shadow of Brandywine
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SOURCES
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Harris, Michael C. Brandywine: A Military History of the Battle that Lost Philadelphia but Saved America, September 11, 1777. El Dorado Hills: Savas Beatie, 2014. The definitive modern military history of the battle, winner of the 2015 American Revolution Round Table of Richmond Book Award and the first full-length scholarly treatment of the engagement in a generation.
McGuire, Thomas J. The Philadelphia Campaign, Volume One: Brandywine and the Fall of Philadelphia. Mechanicsburg: Stackpole Books, 2006. The most comprehensive narrative account of the full 1777 Philadelphia Campaign, covering the Brandywine battle in granular tactical detail.
Fischer, David Hackett. Washington's Crossing. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2004. Essential for understanding Washington's strategic evolution from Long Island through Brandywine and into the Trenton-Princeton campaign that followed.
Lengel, Edward G. General George Washington: A Military Life. New York: Random House, 2005. The authoritative modern military biography of Washington, with detailed analysis of his intelligence failures and command decisions at Brandywine.
Smith, Samuel Stelle. The Battle of Brandywine. Monmouth Beach: Philip Freneau Press, 1976. An earlier but carefully researched tactical account that remains a standard reference for troop positions and movement timings.
Ward, Christopher. The War of the Revolution. 2 volumes. New York: MacMillan, 1952. The foundational comprehensive military history of the Revolutionary War, with full coverage of the Philadelphia Campaign and its strategic consequences.
Ferling, John. Almost a Miracle: The American Victory in the War of Independence. New York: Oxford University Press, 2007. Places Brandywine within the full arc of the war, tracing the strategic consequences through Saratoga and the French alliance.
"Battle of Brandywine." George Washington's Mount Vernon Digital Encyclopedia. The George Washington Presidential Library. www.mountvernon.org/library/digitalhistory/digital-encyclopedia/article/battle-of-brandywine
"The Brandywine Campaign of 1777." George Washington's Mount Vernon. Interview with Michael C. Harris. www.mountvernon.org/george-washington/the-revolutionary-war/washingtons-revolutionary-war-battles/the-battle-of-brandywine/the-brandywine-campaign-of-1777
Ewald, Johann. Diary of the American War. Translated and edited by Joseph P. Tustin. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1979. First-person account from a Hessian officer who fought at Brandywine, providing ground-level detail of the British advance and the fighting at Chadds Ford.
"Battle of Brandywine." Encyclopaedia Britannica. www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Brandywine
Townsend, Joseph. Some Account of the British Army Under the Command of General Howe, and of the Battle of Brandywine. Philadelphia: Townsend Ward, 1846. A primary eyewitness account from a Quaker resident of Chester County who observed the battle and the movements of both armies on September 11, 1777.

snippet.description:

The true story of La Llorona begins with an Aztec goddess who wailed through the streets of Tenochtitlan a decade before the Spanish arrived.
From the Florentine Codex to Chavela Vargas, from Hernán Cortés to the canals of Xochimilco, this is the weeping woman as you've never heard her story.

For five hundred years, people across the Americas have heard the same cry echoing near rivers and canals: "Ay, mis hijos." Oh, my children. The story most people know tells of María, a beautiful woman who drowned her children after her husband's betrayal and now wanders the waterways forever. But the legend runs far deeper than this colonial-era tale.

This documentary traces La Llorona back to her true origins: the sixth of eight omens recorded by Aztec priests before the Spanish conquest. We explore Cihuacoatl, the skull-faced serpent goddess who wept for children who would be lost, and the Cihuateteo, spirits of women who died in childbirth and returned to steal living children. We examine how La Malinche, Cortés's interpreter and the mother of one of the first mestizo children, became entangled with the legend. And we follow La Llorona as she traveled north with Spanish colonization, adapting to new landscapes from Santa Fe's acequias to the Rio Grande borderlands.

La Llorona endures because she is more than a ghost story. She is the grief of the conquest made manifest, a warning to children about dangerous water, and a symbol of what society has done to women across centuries. Her cry carries the weight of five hundred years of loss, and she will keep crying as long as anyone listens.

#LaLlorona #MexicanFolklore #WeepingWoman

snippet.title: The Most Dangerous Nazi: Rise, Terror and the Assassination of Reinhard Heydrich
snippet.description:
He was dismissed from the German Navy over a love triangle. He bluffed his way into the most dangerous intelligence job in the Reich using nothing but spy novels he had read as a boy. And within a decade, he was chairing the meeting that coordinated the murder of millions. The rise of Reinhard Heydrich is one of the most chilling stories of the entire Nazi era, not because he was a monster from the beginning, but because of how deliberately, ruthlessly, and efficiently he made himself into one. This is the inside story of how a disgraced, unemployed nobody climbed to the very top of Hitler's inner circle, outmaneuvered rivals who feared him, orchestrated the Holocaust as a bid for personal power, and was finally brought down by a pair of assassins on a Prague street corner on May 27th, 1942. And the question of who really let him die, the British agents who bombed his car or the man who sent his own doctor to treat him, has never been fully answered.

snippet.title: After the Empire: The Forgotten Corners of Britain's Colonial Legacy | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
It was the largest empire the world has ever seen. At its peak in 1920, the British Empire covered a quarter of the earth's surface, backed by the most powerful navy in history. Then it dissolved, and what it left behind tells a story that no history book quite captures. A hospital that nursed sailors back from Trafalgar and the Falklands, now being sold off as luxury flats. A Caribbean island buried under volcanic ash, still waiting for the mother country to truly show up. A fishing community at the edge of the world, where the last family sat alone for six weeks after everyone else had already gone. Three forsaken places. Three stories about what it really means when an empire ends, and the people who are still living with the consequences.

snippet.title: All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO): a Duality in Mission Regarding UAPs (Sean Kirkpatrick)
snippet.description:
AARO was a Congressionally mandated organization with two missions: 1. organize, streamline, collate, and investigate current reports of military and government sightings of unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), and 2. Investigate the US Government's historical works and associated whistleblower accounts regarding UAP/UFO. This presentation will discuss the establishment of the office, the investigations into the allegations, and the associated findings and conclusions.

Dr. Sean Kirkpatrick is an American laser and materials physicist who served as the first director of the United States Department of Defense's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office. Kirkpatrick is also an adjunct assistant professor of physics at the University of Georgia.

In this talk, Dr. Kirkpatrick explains how AARO approached the investigation of unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP)—including military sightings, historical cases, and whistleblower claims about UFOs.

This presentation covers:
How the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office was created and what Congress tasked it to do
How UAP reports from pilots, radar systems, and sensors are analyzed
What AARO found when reviewing decades of U.S. government UFO investigations
The role of data, physics, and intelligence analysis in evaluating extraordinary claims
Common misconceptions about UAP, including sensor errors, balloons, and airborne clutter

Dr. Kirkpatrick also discusses the challenges of separating unknown phenomena from misidentified objects, and what current evidence does—and does not—support regarding UAP.

Views expressed in this video are those of the speaker and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Capital Area Skeptics.

snippet.title: The End Of The West? How China Is Taking Over The World
snippet.description:

snippet.title: The Entire History of Afghanistan Empire - Full Detailed Documentary
snippet.description: Travel the mountain corridors and caravan roads that made Afghanistan the hinge of continents. This documentary traces a clear, chronological arc from Achaemenid Ariana and Hellenistic Bactria through the Kushan synthesis and the Persianate-Islamic turn. Watch frontier garrisons become capitals under the Ghaznavids, see highland power surge with the Ghurids, and feel the Mongol shock before Timurid Herat glows with art and learning. Follow the triple contest of Safavids, Uzbeks, and Mughals over Kabul and Kandahar, the Hotak revolt that toppled a great dynasty, and the Durrani founding that forged an Afghan empire. Then step into modern statecraft: Barakzai consolidation, the three Anglo Afghan wars, border making, and reformers who tried to build schools, courts, and roads. The twentieth century closes with revolution, occupation, resistance, and the hard aftermath. Throughout, we focus on cause and effect, why geography matters, how administrations worked, and what changed for ordinary people in markets, mosques, and fields. If you want a fact based, human centered narrative that explains not only what happened but why it mattered, this is your guided tour through the crossroads of empires.

snippet.title: Lynn Rothschild | Nature’s Hardware Store: Building the Future with Biology
snippet.description:
In her Long Now Talk, NASA researcher Dr. Lynn Rothschild explores how the extreme constraints of space travel can enable radical sustainability on Earth.

Hear how her teams have used mycelium, the root structure of fungi, to grow off-planet construction materials, and programmed bacteria to print new biological materials on demand.

Cells, Rothschild explains, are micromachines with a 3.8-billion-year R&D history. Her research harnesses these ancient biological processes to engineer living systems that make tools, materials, and medicines that could sustain astronauts and settlements beyond Earth.

This talk was presented October 14, 02025 at the Cowell Theater in San Francisco. 

Episode notes: https://longnow.org/talks/02025-rothschild/

The event livestream is here: https://youtube.com/live/8435j107Yp8

By inspiring thought and conversation about how we've been shaped by the last 10,000 years and what might be in store for us over the next 10,000 years, Long Now Talks seek to expand our collective sense of the present moment. Long Now Talks cover futurism and speculative fiction; time, nature, and contemplative practices; the intersection of the humanities and sciences; the evolution of counterculture to cyberculture; cultural imagination, land art and public monuments; and of course, long-term thinking and being a good ancestor.

snippet.title: Bayo Akomolafe | The Untimely
snippet.description:
In his Talk, poet-philosopher Bayo Akomolafe presented a riveting critique of linear time, and gave a persuasive invitation to step sideways, to slow down, to notice the cracks in our temporal systems. 

Through Yoruba cosmology, slave ship histories, and decolonization strategies, he invited us to look at the space between the tick and the tock, to sit in the uncomfortable and incomplete. Only here, in what Akomolafe calls “parapolitics of the untimely,” can we ask, “What does untimeliness make possible?”

This talk was presented May 5, 02026 at the Cowell Theater in San Francisco.
